title: Getting Started with Arduino
subtitle: IDE, sketch structure, uploading code, and non-blocking timing
author: Kernal Team

whyItExists.problem: Writing embedded C/C++ from scratch requires setting up toolchains, linker scripts, and startup code. Beginners need a simpler on-ramp that hides that complexity without limiting what they can eventually build.
whyItExists.solution: Arduino provides a beginner-friendly IDE, a cross-platform C++ wrapper (the Wire/Serial/Digital APIs), and one-click compile & upload — letting you focus on the application logic rather than toolchain setup.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Prototyping, learning embedded, quick one-off projects, and any time the Arduino library ecosystem covers your needs.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Mass-production or complex multi-task firmware where you need PlatformIO, bare-metal HAL drivers, or a proper RTOS.

explainModes.beginner: Arduino is like a template for embedded programs. Every sketch has two boxes: setup() runs once when you plug it in, and loop() runs over and over forever. You write your code inside those boxes and click Upload to send it to the board.
explainModes.simple: An Arduino sketch is a C++ program with a simplified API. setup() initialises hardware once; loop() is an infinite while(true) loop. The IDE compiles your sketch to machine code and uploads it via USB. delay() pauses execution for milliseconds.
explainModes.standard: Arduino wraps avr-gcc / arm-gcc compilation, linking against the Arduino core library. main() is hidden — it calls setup() once, then loops calling loop() forever. Libraries are installed via the Library Manager and included with #include.
explainModes.technical: The Arduino build system invokes avr-g++ with -mmcu=atmega328p -DF_CPU=16000000UL -Os. The core provides digital/analog I/O via PORT register writes wrapped in digitalWrite() etc. HardwareSerial uses UART interrupt buffers; delay() uses Timer0 overflow counting millis().
explainModes.deepDive: The linker script places .text in flash at 0x0000, .data at SRAM start (copied from flash by startup code), .bss zeroed by startup code. The vector table occupies the first 52 bytes. F() macro uses __FlashStringHelper to prevent SRAM copying of string literals. PlatformIO offers the same toolchain with CMake-style project management, library dependency resolution, and unit testing.

content.text: The Arduino IDE and Sketch Structure

Every Arduino program is called a sketch (file extension .ino). The structure is rigid: two mandatory functions — setup() and loop(). Install Arduino IDE 2 from arduino.cc, select your board (Tools → Board → Arduino Uno), select your COM port, and click the Upload arrow.

Libraries extend Arduino with ready-made drivers for sensors, displays, and protocols. Install them via the Library Manager (Sketch → Include Library → Manage Libraries) or by placing a folder in your Arduino libraries directory. After installing, include with #include <LibraryName.h>.

delay() blocks everything — no sensor readings, no button checks, no serial data. For anything beyond the simplest blink, use millis() (milliseconds since boot) to track elapsed time without halting the program.

Avoid delay() in production sketches — it blocks everything for the duration. Use the millis() pattern above to run multiple tasks 'simultaneously'. The same pattern works for debouncing, sensor polling, and heartbeat LEDs.

Arduino's Serial Monitor (Ctrl+Shift+M) is your primary debugging tool. It shows messages sent via Serial.print() and lets you send commands from your PC. Always ensure the Serial Monitor baud rate matches Serial.begin() — a mismatch shows garbled characters.

On Arduino Uno, pins 0 (RX) and 1 (TX) are shared with USB serial. Using them for other hardware while also using Serial.print() will corrupt both. Reserve pins 0/1 for USB debug; use SoftwareSerial on other pins for additional serial devices.

questions.question: How many times does setup() run in a typical Arduino sketch?
options: Once at power-on or after each reset
questions.explanation: setup() runs exactly once at power-on or after a reset. All hardware initialisation goes here. loop() then runs continuously.

questions.question: Why should you prefer millis() over delay() in production code?
options: millis() is more accurate for timing
delay() blocks all processing; millis() lets you do other work between events
questions.explanation: delay() freezes the CPU — no button reads, no sensor samples, no serial data processed. millis() checks elapsed time without blocking, enabling multiple independent timed tasks in one loop.

questions.question: What does the F() macro do?
options: Formats floating-point numbers with 2 decimal places
Stores string literals in flash memory instead of SRAM
Converts an integer to a float
questions.explanation: F("string") stores the string literal in flash (program memory) instead of copying it to precious SRAM. Essential on 2 KB SRAM Arduino Uno to avoid running out of RAM with many strings.

faq.q: Can I write Arduino code in pure C++ without the .ino wrapper?
faq.a: Yes. Arduino sketches compile as C++. You can use all C++ features, STL (carefully — SRAM is limited), templates, classes, and namespaces. The .ino extension just means the IDE auto-adds #include <Arduino.h>.

faq.q: What is PlatformIO and when should I use it instead of the Arduino IDE?
faq.a: PlatformIO is a professional IDE extension (VS Code) for embedded development. It supports 1000+ boards, dependency management (like npm for Arduino libraries), unit testing, and CI/CD. Use it for any project larger than a weekend prototype.

faq.q: My millis() wraps around after 49 days — will that break my code?
faq.a: Only if you use ==, >, or < comparisons. The pattern `if (now - lastEvent >= interval)` is rollover-safe because unsigned subtraction handles the wrap correctly. Never compare with ==; always use >=.
